planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil in partial shade in spring; this Southeastern piedmont native tolerates more sun than its northern relative W. ternata as long as soil moisture stays consistent.

directions: A rare rocky-riverbank native of the Georgia and Carolina piedmont, this Waldsteinia forms a low, spreading evergreen mat of glossy, deeply lobed and toothed leaves that turn burgundy through winter and flush fresh green again each spring. Small, petal-reduced yellow flowers appear in early spring, followed by dry brown fruit; the display is subtle and foliage-driven rather than floral. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes into a dense weed-suppressing carpet on shaded slopes and stream banks, and unlike many groundcovers it accepts brief full-sun exposure provided the acidic, well-drained soil never dries out completely. Best used as a specimen or small-scale groundcover in native woodland plantings rather than large-area coverage, since it spreads more slowly than common barren strawberry.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; brighter shade helps preserve the leaf variegation without scorching.

directions: This selection of the East Asian groundcover Reineckia carnea carries the same grassy, arching, rhizome-spreading habit as the species but with each glossy dark-green leaf edged or striped in creamy white, giving the low evergreen mat a brighter presence in dim woodland corners. Short spikes of small, fragrant pink flowers appear near the base of the foliage in late summer, followed by red berries. It performs identically to the plain species as a slow, tidy, weed-suppressing edger or small-scale groundcover under trees, tolerating the same dry-shade root competition, but the variegated foliage is more valued as a foliage accent than for mass coverage since it is slower to spread than solid-green forms.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this vigorous selection spreads readily by rhizomes into a dense running mat over several seasons.

directions: 'Greenscape' is a Plant Delights Nursery selection of Reineckia carnea chosen for its vigor, producing long, narrow, glossy dark-green leaves on a mat that spreads more assertively by rhizome than the typical species, making it useful as a true running groundcover rather than a slow-clumping accent. In late fall it sends up short spikes of pale lavender flowers close to the foliage, followed by small lavender-toned fruit. Grown for its dense, mondo-grass-like texture in shaded beds, it fills in dry, root-filled ground under trees where turf fails, and functions as an evergreen, low-maintenance alternative to liriope in warmer zones. Division is only needed to control spread rather than to renew vigor.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden catalog

planting.note: Transplant rooted stem cuttings or small clumps into moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade in spring, exactly as for the typical red-berried species.

directions: This naturally occurring form of the native woodland groundcover partridgeberry is identical to the typical species in habit, foliage, and paired fragrant white summer flowers, differing only in producing ivory-white rather than scarlet-red fruit come autumn. Like the species, it forms a tight, trailing, evergreen mat of small round glossy leaves across acidic forest-floor soil, and the pale berries persist into winter, offering an unusual color variant for collectors of native shade plants and woodland terrariums. It requires the same demanding conditions as the species: deep shade, constantly moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil, and is best sited in a prepared bed under oaks or conifers rather than typical garden soil. Because the white-fruited form is uncommon in the wild, plants are typically propagated by cuttings or division from known stock rather than seed to preserve the trait.

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or plant container stock into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; the silvered foliage pattern is most vivid in cooler weather and in brighter shade.

directions: Discovered by Dan Heims of Terra Nova Nurseries within a wild population of the Pacific Northwest native fringecups, 'Forest Frost' carries a striking silver overlay across its rounded, scalloped, heuchera-like leaves that deepens to bronzy, quilted tones through fall and winter. In spring it sends up the same slender flowering wands as the species, lined with small fringed chartreuse blooms that fade to pink as they age. It tolerates deeper shade and more drought than most silver-leaved perennials once established, making it a reliable foliage plant for dry shade under trees where flower color is secondary to season-long leaf interest. Divide every few years to maintain vigor and to propagate true to the silvered pattern, since seedlings do not reliably inherit the variegation.

planting.note: Plant divisions or runner-produced plantlets in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; unlike its smaller relatives this species is fully evergreen and tolerates somewhat drier soil than typical Chrysosplenium.

directions: Native to Chinese woodlands, this is the largest and most garden-worthy member of the golden saxifrage genus, forming a low evergreen carpet of rounded, primrose-like leaves in dark grey-green flushed with bronzy red, most pronounced in cold weather. It spreads by long, non-invasive runners that root and form new plantlets in the manner of a strawberry, gradually knitting together into a dense mat. In late winter and early spring it produces clusters of small, faintly fragrant greenish-white flowers with conspicuous pink-tipped stamens, an unusually showy display for the genus. It is still uncommon in North American cultivation but is prized by shade-garden specialists for year-round foliage interest where consistently moist, humus-rich soil can be provided.
